content: Thiabendazole, also known by its International Nonproprietary Name (INN) and British Approved Name (BAN), as well as its American Adopted Name (AAN) and United States Adopted Name (USAN), is a compound with antifungal and antiparasitic properties. It is marketed under trade names such as Mintezol, Tresaderm, and Arbotect. This substance is utilized as a fungicide for agricultural purposes, such as protecting fruits (e.g., oranges) and vegetables, and as a prophylactic treatment for Dutch elm disease. Additionally, its use in the treatment of aspergillosis has been documented. As an antiparasitic agent, thiabendazole is effective in controlling various helminths, including roundworms (e.g., those causing strongyloidiasis), hookworms, and other parasitic species that infect humans, livestock, and wild animals. Thiabendazole also functions as an angiogenesis inhibitor. It has been demonstrated to block angiogenesis in vertebrates by targeting genes responsible for maintaining yeast cell walls. This effect has been observed in both frog embryos and human cells. Furthermore, it acts as a vascular-disrupting agent, reducing newly formed blood vessels, and has shown efficacy in certain cancer cell types. Pharmacodynamically, thiabendazole exerts its effects by inhibiting fumarate reductase, a mitochondrial enzyme specific to helminths. This inhibition may involve interactions with endogenous quinones. Medically, thiabendazole serves as a chelating agent, binding to metals in cases of metal poisoning, such as lead, mercury, or antimony toxicity. In veterinary medicine, it is used to treat ear infections in dogs and cats. Additionally, it is employed as a food additive and preservative, designated with the E number E233 (INS number 233). For instance, it is applied to bananas to maintain freshness and is a common component in the wax coatings of citrus fruit skins. However, its use as a food additive is not approved in the European Union, Australia, or New Zealand. Regarding safety, thiabendazole exhibits slight toxicity at higher doses. In test animals, high exposure levels have been associated with liver and intestinal disorders, as well as reproductive issues and reduced weaning weights. In humans, adverse effects from therapeutic use may include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, diarrhea, dizziness, drowsiness, and headache. Rarely, it may cause tinnitus, vision changes, abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine, fever, fatigue, increased thirst, or changes in urinary output. Carcinogenic effects have been observed at higher doses.
